claims.claim: A schedule can specify when planned work will be performed and show when major events are expected, so a milestone can make a significant project point visible without describing every activity around it.
A task describes planned work, whereas a deliverable is a result of work and a milestone is a significant event or point; these categories can be connected without being interchangeable.
A schedule can provide a reference for comparing performance against an approved plan, but an entry in a plan alone is not evidence that a milestone occurred.
A decision point can be communicated as a meaningful event requiring attention without implying that the schedule determines who has authority or which outcome must be chosen.

Clear milestone status communication distinguishes a planned event, evidence that an event occurred, and unresolved conditions; it improves the inspectability of current project information without guaranteeing results.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The source materials treat scheduling within professional and government frameworks that include detailed controls and analysis, while this lesson is introductory and centered on communication.
positions: GAO discusses a reliable schedule as a management tool, including major events and comparison against an approved plan.
PMI provides professional standards, practice guides, and terminology for scheduling and project management.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson retains only general concepts of a milestone as a significant point, the distinction from tasks and deliverables, appropriate evidence, and honest status communication. It does not prescribe a tool, calculate a schedule, or assign organizational authority.

unsupportedExistingClaims: A generic draft could call every task a milestone, equate a calendar entry with an achieved event, or imply that a decision-point label automatically grants authority or resolves an issue.
correctionsNeeded: Uses original prose and a clearly labeled hypothetical library example rather than reproducing source templates or diagrams.
Separates work, results, and events, and distinguishes planned from achieved milestones through the role of evidence.
Keeps scheduling calculation, critical-path analysis, estimation depth, and organization-specific procedures outside the lesson.
rightsIssues: PMI materials were checked live and are treated as REFERENCE_ONLY; no PMI prose, templates, diagrams, or standards text is reproduced.
